title: Preparing to meet Him
hook: whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him; and Aisha's honest question
tomorrow: what should be on your mind at the very end?

segments.voice: Yesterday: just passing. A traveler with a light bag, kind to the people on the road. But a road ends somewhere, at someone.

Before a first date, or meeting someone's parents, there's a ritual. The shower, the clean shirt, a little scent at the wrist, one more look in the mirror. You get ready because the meeting matters. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari answers yesterday's question with a meeting: whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him, and whoever dislikes meeting Allah, Allah dislikes meeting him. Loving the end of the road? That sounds impossible. Someone in the room said so, out loud.
screen: `THE SHOWER, THE CLEAN SHIRT.` → `WHOEVER LOVES TO MEET ALLAH.` → `SOMEONE SAID: IMPOSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: It was Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In the report she says, plainly: but we all dislike death. And he answers: it isn't that. When a believer's time comes, he is given good news of Allah's mercy and pleasure, and then nothing is dearer to him than what lies ahead. So the hadith doesn't ask anyone to like dying, and Aisha's honest question stays in the record. It's about the meeting, and whether you've been getting ready for someone you love. In Islam, getting ready often runs through the senses. Before every prayer, wudu: water on the hands, the mouth, the face. Before Friday prayer, a report in Bukhari mentions washing, cleaning the teeth with a miswak, and wearing scent if you have it. The body rehearses standing before Allah, again and again. Preparing to meet Him, then, isn't a grim project. It looks like any meeting with someone you love: wash, put on something clean, think about what you'll say, settle what's unsettled. Notice the shape of the sentence: the love runs both ways.
screen: `AISHA: WE ALL DISLIKE DEATH.` · `IT ISN'T THAT: GOOD NEWS.` · `WATER, A TOOTH-STICK, SCENT.` · `READY, LIKE ANY MEETING.` · then, large: `LOVES TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: If there's soap and water near you, or a little scent, use it now. Wash your hands slowly, or touch a drop of scent to your wrist, and notice the cool of the water or the smell as you breathe. While you do, name one thing you'd want settled before a meeting that matters: a call you owe, a word you haven't said.
screen: `WATER OR SCENT.` · `NOTICE THE SMELL, THE COOL.` · `ONE THING TO HAVE READY.`

segments.voice: Preparing to meet Him: getting ready for the meeting with Allah the way you'd get ready to meet someone you love. Clean, settled, and glad to go.
Keep this one close: loves to meet him, a love the hadith says runs both ways. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1768 COUNTS.` → `THE JOURNEY HOME · 3 OF 11.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT SHOULD BE ON YOUR MIND AT THE END?`

howItsDone: Muslims prepare for prayer with wudu, and for Friday prayer by washing, cleaning the teeth and wearing scent if they have it; teachers often pair this hadith with the idea that a whole life can be a getting-ready to meet Allah.

fork.setup: your uncle admits he dreads death and feels guilty about it, because he's heard 'the believer loves to meet Allah.' what did the Prophet say to the same worry?
options: it isn't about liking death; at the end, the believer gets good news.
real believers never fear death, so he should work on his faith.
the hadith is only about scholars and saints, not ordinary people.
fork.reveal: Aisha raised exactly this: we all dislike death. his answer: it isn't that. at the end comes good news of mercy, and then the meeting is wanted.

original.note: Arabic: meeting Allah; the phrase at the heart of this hadith.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving to meet Allah means wanting to die.
what it means: getting ready for the meeting with Allah like any meeting with someone you love; Aisha's 'we all dislike death' is answered, not scolded.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 6507 and Muslim 2684, liqa' Allah and Aisha's question; the senses of preparation in wudu and the Friday sunnah of washing, miswak and scent (Bukhari 880).
guess: getting ready for the meeting with Allah, as for someone loved
keeping your will and funeral plans updated each year
praying extra in the days just before someone dies

chat.says: Dadi asked me to help write down her wishes, like a will. she keeps making jokes. i can't laugh
options: Maybe she's at ease because she's getting ready, like for a meeting she wants. Ask her.
Then she must think it's soon. People don't write those things unless they're sick.
Joking means she isn't taking death seriously, and that's what the hadith warns about.
chat.meaning: In the hadith, preparing to meet Allah is like getting ready to meet someone you love. Getting ready isn't the same as being near the end.

Aisha.meaning: a wife of the Prophet who reported many of his words

wudu.meaning: washing hands, mouth, face and more before prayer

miswak.meaning: a twig used to clean the teeth

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of reports of the Prophet's words and deeds

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6507 (also Sahih Muslim 2684): whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him; Aisha says we all dislike death; the Prophet answers that at death the believer is given good news of Allah's mercy and pleasure
Sahih al-Bukhari 880: on Friday, washing, cleaning the teeth with a miswak, and using scent if available
